document.title: Comments and Protest of FirstEnergy Service Company re PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.'s 07/31/2026 filing proposing to establish a Reliability Backstop…

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION  
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.   
    ) 
 
Docket No. ER26-3380-000
COMMENTS AND PROTEST OF  
FIRSTENERGY SERVICE COMPANY 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”),1 FirstEnergy Service Company 
(“FirstEnergy”) respectfully submits these comments and protest of the filing submitted by 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) on July 31, 2026, proposing to establish a Reliability 
Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) mechanism.2
FirstEnergy agrees that new generation is needed.  Unfortunately, fundamental 
elements of PJM’s RBP proposal are fatally flawed and as a result these elements cannot 
be approved consistent with Section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”).  Section 205 
of the FPA provides that the Commission can accept PJM’s RBP proposal only if it is just 
and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.3  The filing utility—PJM—
bears the burden of proof to demonstrate its proposal meets these FPA requirements.4  The 
Commission may accept PJM’s proposal only if there is sufficient evidence in the record 
to show PJM has carried its Section 205 burden of proof.5  The Commission will reject any 
1

2
PJM Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns Stemming from 
Large Loads, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 (“July 31 RBP Proposal”). 
3
16 U.S.C. § 824d(a)-(b). 
4
Constellation Mystic Power, LLC v. FERC,  45 F.4th 1028, 1035 (D.C. Cir. 2022); NorthWestern

Operator, Inc., 194 FERC ¶ 61,050, at P 23 (2026); Calpine Corp. v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 163 FERC 
¶ 61,236, at P 7 (2018). 
5
Northwestern Corp., 884 F.3d at 1182-84; City of Winnfield v. FERC, 744 F.2d 871, 876-77 (D.C. 
Cir. 1984); NorthWestern Corp., 147 FERC ¶ 61,049, at P 48 (2014).

2 
proposal that falls outside the zone of reasonableness—i.e., does not result in just and 
reasonable rates in accordance with Section 205.6  Moreover, even if a rate falls within the 
zone of reasonableness, it may nevertheless violate Section 205 due to being unduly 
discriminatory or preferential.7
In these comments and protest, FirstEnergy demonstrates that PJM’s filing does not 
meet the FPA Section 205 just and reasonable standard because: 
1. PJM did not follow the Statement of Principles policy directive for 
determining how much new capacity to purchase, or how to allocate the 
costs;8
2. PJM's load-side collateral requirements are unsupported and not 
necessary;   
3. PJM's levelized contract framework – which permits suppliers to “front 
load” the capacity contracts – creates unnecessary affordability risks; 
4. PJM’s proposed cost allocation can result in costs not going to new data 
centers as required by the Statement of Principles and also fails to 
comply with fundamental cost allocation criteria; 
5. PJM’s Reliability Backstop Procurement should be limited to resources 
that most effectively address reliability needs;  
6. PJM's proposed implementation schedule is compressed unreasonably; 
7. PJM’s proposed “opt-out” mechanism allows for unreasonable cost 
shifting; 
8. FERC should direct PJM to strengthen supplier performance and credit 
requirements; and 
9. FERC should direct PJM to clarify that its proposed gating criteria 
require binding contractual commitments for eligible demand response 
resources. 
In addition to the above, FirstEnergy respectfully submits that FERC should require 
that, when PJM refiles tariff amendments that comply with the Statement of Principles,

423 (2021)).

Ala. Elec. Co-op., Inc. v. FERC, 684 F.2d 20, 27 (D.C. Cir. 1982) (citing U.S. v. Ill. Cent. R.R., 263 
U.S. 515, 524 (1924)). 
8
Statement of Principles Regarding PJM, National Energy Dominance Council (Jan. 16, 2026),
available at https://www.energy.gov/documents/statement-principles-regarding-pjm[https://perma.cc/35HJ-
W56E](the “Statement” or “Statement of Principles”).

3 
PJM should provide certain clarifications about the qualifications and criteria for Demand 
Response to participate in the backstop procurement. 
COMMENTS AND PROTEST 
1. 
PJM Did Not Follow the Statement of Principles Policy 
Directive For Determining How Much New Capacity to 
Purchase, or How to Allocate the Costs. 
The Statement of Principles directs PJM to conduct a reliability backstop auction 
to procure new capacity resources, with the procurement to provide a 15-year term of price 
certainty.9  The Statement also directs that the costs are to be allocated to load-serving 
entities with new data centers that have not self-procured new capacity or agreed to be 
curtailable.10  PJM’s proposal makes no effort to comply with this directive.  Instead, PJM 
proposes to allocate costs based on forecasts that were submitted in 2025.  PJM does not 
identify the data centers that are included in such forecasts, nor does it make any effort to 
ensure that the costs that are so allocated go only to new data centers that have not self-
supplied or agreed to be curtailable.  As such, PJM cannot demonstrate that the costs will 
go to new data centers. 
PJM cannot justify its failure to adhere to the Statement’s policy guidance.  The 
Statement was issued on January 16, 2026 and PJM’s filing was submitted on July 31, 
2026.  PJM had six and one-half months to identify the new data centers that are within 
scope, and to hold stakeholder discussions for how to allocate the costs at the wholesale 
and retail level.  PJM did not do so.  Instead, PJM conducted extensive stakeholder 
processes in an effort to justify its preferred policy direction, and then refused to implement 
9
Statement of Principles, Bullet 1.  Notably, PJM’s proposal does not comply even with this 
straightforward directive as it contemplates that resources may contract for terms of less than 15 years. 
10
Id., Bullet 3.

4 
the stakeholder-endorsed backstop procurement proposal that came out of that process.11
In other words, PJM ran out the clock with stakeholder processes instead of utilizing the 
allotted time to solicit the data that would be necessary for PJM to allocate the backstop 
procurement costs as directed by the Statement of Principles. 
PJM cannot take refuge in its broad authority to amend the terms of the existing 
Reliability Assurance Agreement.12  It’s correct to say that Section 16.4 of the RAA gives 
the PJM Board broad rights to amend the agreement.  And it’s also correct to say that 
Section 16.4 of Attachment DD of the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“OATT”) 
describes a “reliability backstop auction.”13  But PJM’s authorization to amend the RAA
and the OATT is subject to certain inherent limiting principles.  PJM cannot, for example, 
create an entirely new power product and impose the costs on wholesale or retail customers 
simply because it wants to or simply because in its best judgement its corporate principles 
will be served. 
Importantly, PJM was not “starting from scratch.”  As noted, the current OATT 
describes a “reliability backstop” product.  The Statement of Principles reflects policy 
guidance and direction from a slate of bipartisan state governors and the White House.  
And the PJM stakeholder process included a “Joint Proposal” by a group of Electric

and Connect and Manage, available at https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-

and-connect-and-manage.pdf.

5 
Distribution Companies and Data Center Customers for how to implement the Statement
and allocate the costs.14
PJM’s proposal is not consistent with any of the above.  Instead, and as noted above 
and throughout this Protest, PJM has submitted tariff amendments that are inconsistent in 
material terms with the Statement of Principles and a proposal that was approved by the 
overwhelming majority of stakeholders.  Even worse, PJM’s tariff amendments call for the 
costs of its backstop procurement to attach before LSEs (and their respective stakeholders) 
will have any meaningful opportunity to avoid such costs by exercising their right to exit.  
That is, PJM proposes to conduct a procurement that it admits it has designed in such a 
manner that the cost likely will be close to the “notational value” (or cap) of $555/MWD, 
or approximately $20.7 billion over the 15-year term of the contracts, and for the 
procurement to be conducted and the costs to attach before LSEs and their stakeholders 
can exercise their right to avoid such costs by exiting.   
There is no scenario where this outcome can be construed as “just and reasonable.”  
Even if the Commission were inclined to approve the proposal—which given the above 
would raise serious doubt about the legal durability of such approval—to do so would bring 
even more uncertainty as LSEs, the PJM states, and other important stakeholders could be 
forced to resort to extraordinary legal measures to prevent such costs from attaching before 
the appellate process could address the merits of the Commission’s action. 
Given the manifest deficiencies in PJM’s filing, and the significant financial and 
legal risk in going forward, the Commission should: (i) rule that PJM has not met its 
14
Available at 20260630-item-02f---joint-edcs-and-data-center-coalition---rbp---executive-
summary.pdf.

6 
statutory “just and reasonable” burden for going forward, and (ii) provide guidance for 
PJM and the stakeholders going forward.  Moreover, in light of the amount of time that has 
passed since the January 16, 2026 issuance of the Statement of Principles, and the 
Commission’s experience with obtaining a broadly-supported outcome for PJM capacity 
issues,15 the Commission should give serious consideration to commencing an FPA Section 
206 proceeding and then facilitating settlement negotiations. 
Speaking to the going-forward process: creation of the Reliability Pricing Model 
(“RPM”) is the analogue for navigating significant policy changes for the PJM capacity 
product.  As the Commission is aware, over twenty years ago, PJM submitted amendments 
to its tariff to implement its vision for funding the capacity cost of physical generation.16
Then, as now, the proposed tariff amendments were poorly designed and faced significant 
opposition from utilities, customers, and state regulators.  The Commission rejected PJM’s 
filing and instituted an FPA Section 20617 proceeding.  There were many months of 
settlement negotiations and, ultimately, the majority of PJM’s stakeholders were able to 
agree, or “not oppose” the RPM construct.18  This background illustrates the arbitrary 
nature of PJM’s current proposal:  less than 20% of the stakeholders voted for PJM’s RBP 
proposal,19 whereas almost 60% of the stakeholders voted in favor of a Joint Electric

Rehearing and Approving Settlement Subject to Conditions, 117 FERC ¶ 61,331 (2006).

Distribution Company/Data Center Coalition proposal.20  The Commission should follow 
the RPM playbook: reject PJM’s filing, institute an FPA Section 206 proceeding, and 
establish settlement proceedings. 
 
2.  
PJM’s 
Proposed 
LSE 
Collateral 
Requirements 
Are 
Unnecessary and Excessive. 
PJM proposes to impose a new and onerous collateral obligation on each LSE 
allocated RBP Charges.21  Under the Proposed Tariff, the cumulative LSE credit 
requirement would initially equal $1.5 million multiplied by the total MW of committed 
RBP Unforced Capacity (“UCAP”) allocated to the LSE.22  PJM has failed to meet its 
burden under section 205 to demonstrate that its proposed LSE credit requirement is just 
and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory and the Commission must therefore reject 
PJM’s unprecedented load-side collateral requirements.   
PJM fails to demonstrate why it is necessary to require LSEs to post additional 
collateral. Retail customers, hopefully the new data centers described in the Statement of 
Principles, ultimately will take these costs.23  Because retail customers ultimately will pay 
the RBP costs, there is no justification for imposing new and onerous collateral 
20
See 6/30/26 PJM Members Committee, Supplemental Voting Results, available at mc-voting-
results---agenda-item-3o---joint-edcs-and-data-center-coalition-rbp-proposal.pdf. 
21
See July 31 RBP Proposal at 108-123. 
22
Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD at Section 18.8(b)(i)(A). 
23
See, e.g., Qualifying Facility Rates & Requirements Implementation Issues Under the Pub. Util. 
Regul. Pol’ys Act of 1978, 172 FERC ¶ 61,041, at P 40 (2020) (recognizing that “electric utilities with 
franchised service territories that make sales at retail are often effectively guaranteed the recovery of their 
energy costs in their retail rates by their state regulatory authorities—provided that such costs are prudently 
incurred.”); Pa. Power Co. v. Pub. Util. Comm’n, 932 A.2d 300 (Pa. Commw. Ct. 2007).

8 
requirements on LSEs that will likely result in hundreds of millions of dollars in additional 
collateral, the costs of which will ultimately be borne by retail ratepayers.24 
PURPA must-purchase arrangements supporting Qualifying Facility development 
are the closest long-term contractual analogue to the sort of commitment that LSEs will be 
required to assume as a result of PJM’s RBP.25  Under PURPA contracts, however, the 
purchasing entities generally have been subject to low or no collateral requirements 
because of their ability to recover costs from retail customers.26  Imposing identical rates, 
terms and conditions on entities that are not similarly situated is no less discriminatory than 
treating similar situated entities differently.27  PJM’s proposal is therefore unduly 
discriminatory and must be rejected. 
Even if some additional collateral was appropriate, PJM must be able to show that 
its proposed collateral requirements are reasonably tailored to the actual credit risk 
presented by specific LSEs, or substantially similar classes of LSEs.  PJM’s proposal is 
unjust and unreasonable because it automatically treats such entities as presenting the same 
nonpayment risk as LSEs without comparable cost-recovery mechanisms.  It does not

9 
explain whether or how regulated cost recovery affects LSE default risk, and it does not 
identify evidence that LSEs with such recovery mechanisms require collateral equal to 
approximately half of a 15-year notional payment stream.   
These deficiencies alone require rejection of PJM’s collateral proposal.  However, 
PJM’s collateral proposal suffers from additional flaws: 

PJM fails to provide sufficient justification for the $1.5 million per MW figure. 
PJM does not identify an expected probability of default, a loss-given-default 
assumption, a historical LSE default experience, a liquidation or replacement 
period, or any other quantitative measure connecting the proposed $1.5 million 
per committed RBP MW requirement to a reasonably anticipated loss. 

PJM acknowledges that LSEs and other market participants already are subject 
to existing collateral requirements, but fails to identify the particular limitation 
in Attachment Q that prevents it from addressing a reasonably measured RBP 
exposure through those existing requirements.   

PJM provides no details specifying how quickly excess collateral must be 
returned.  PJM’s proposal to retain absolute discretion to make such 
determinations is unjust and unreasonable as it fails to protect LSEs from over-
collateralization. 

If seller collateral remains available when an RBP Seller defaults, PJM should 
be required to draw upon that collateral and use the proceeds to provide the 
corresponding shortfall credits to the affected LSEs.  Nothing in PJM’s proposal 
explains why the use of available seller collateral should be discretionary, or 
why the proposed tariff provisions are silent regarding the amount, timing, and 
allocation of any proceeds recovered from such collateral. 
In an age of increasing affordability concerns, PJM’s proposal will harm retail 
customers, because those customers will ultimately bear the costs of these credit 
requirements.  Absent more compelling justifications than those contained in the current 
RBP Proposal, the Commission cannot accept PJM’s proposal as within the zone of 
reasonableness.

10 
3.
PJM’s Levelized Contract Framework—Which Permits 
Suppliers to “Front Load” the Capacity Contracts—Creates 
Unnecessary Affordability Risks. 
PJM proposes to clear offers in the RBP Auction based on a levelized cost 
approach.  PJM bears the burden to show it is just and reasonable.  It cannot, and its 
approach creates the risk of excessive affordability concerns for retail ratepayers.   
Specifically, PJM proposes that the levelized cost of all selected RBP offers will 
not exceed a maximum “willingness to pay” of $555/MW-day, on a MW-weighted average 
basis over all of the Delivery Years of the RBP.28  As PJM acknowledges, this means sellers 
can offer substantially different price offers between Delivery Years, so long as the total 
MW-weighted average of all RBP offers over all of the Delivery Years of the RBP does 
not exceed $555-day.29
The predictable consequence of this flexibility is that sellers will front-load their 
costs into the initial years of their contracts, significantly increasing bill impacts in the near 
term.  A seller, for example, could charge $1,000/MW-day for the first several years of the 
contract, and then balance that out with sub-market prices in the latter years.  The result is 
that customers will be forced to bear what could be extremely large increases in capacity 
costs during the initial Delivery Years of the RBP.  All during a period when there is 
increasing concern, including concern by members of this Commission,30 about 
affordability.  Absent a persuasive justification for this levelized offer structure—and there 
is none—the Commission should reject it. 
28
July 31 RBP Proposal at 61-64; Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD at Section 18.5(f). 
29
July 31 RBP Proposal at 62-63. 
30
See, e.g., United States House of Representatives, Committee on Energy & Commerce, 2/3/2026 
Hearing:  Oversight of FERC: Advancing Affordable and Reliable Energy for All Americans, comments of 
Commission members.

11 
A “levelized” cost structure is not needed.  The Statement of Principles calls for 
PJM to provide for price certainty for a 15-year term.31  There is significant investment in 
new generation in areas outside of PJM by vertically-integrated utilities where cost 
recovery generally is on a straight-line fixed value basis.  And the country’s experience 
with PURPA contracts reflects that, generally, nonincumbent utility investors are willing 
to construct new generation on a straight-line fixed value basis.  Doubtless, these factors 
influenced the Statement of Principles policy directive that PJM was to provide price 
certainty for a 15-year term. 
As a “levelized” cost structure is not needed, and as permitting it could lead to 
unacceptable affordability issues, PJM has not carried its FPA Section 205 “just and 
reasonable” burden for going forward.  Accordingly, the Commission should reject PJM’s 
proposed amendments. 
4.
PJM Has Failed to Demonstrate That Its Cost Allocation 
Proposal Is Just and Reasonable. 
PJM proposes that RBP costs will be allocated to LSEs within the territories of 
Electric Distributors.32  Each Electric Distributor’s territory’s share of RBP costs will be 
its pro rata share of the difference between the forecasted load adjustments for the 
2026/2027 and 2028/2029 capacity auction cycles.33  Each Electric Distributor’s territory’s 
share will then be allocated to LSEs within that territory.34   
31
Statement of Principles, Bullet 1. 
32
See July 31 RBP Proposal at 96-97. 
33
Id. at 96-97. 
34
Id. at 97-98.

12 
This proposal is at odds with FPA Section 205 as well as fundamental principles of 
cost allocation.  First, PJM’s cost allocation proposal is not meaningfully targeted to ensure 
the customers ultimately allocated the costs of the RBP will be entities causing the need 
for the procurement of new generation—i.e. new data center customers, in accordance with 
the Statement of Principles.  Rather than proposing an allocation methodology specifically 
targeted to new data centers, PJM instead proposes allocating the costs based on forecasted 
Load Adjustments for the 2026/2026 and 2028/2029 Delivery Years.  These forecasted 
Load Adjustments are not, however, limited to new data centers.  Instead, they include 
facilities with existing contracts and possibly even those already under construction, as 
well as potentially native non-data load customers as well.  In short, PJM is proposing to 
allocate the costs of the new generation needed for tomorrow’s data centers to yesterday’s 
customers.  PJM fails to explain its departure from the Statement of Principles, and 
therefore fails to meet its burden under FPA Section 205 to demonstrate its cost allocation 
proposal is just and reasonable. 
PJM’s proposal is also inconsistent with the Commission’s fundamental cost 
allocation principles, particularly the requirement that costs be assigned “roughly 
commensurate” with the benefits received by customers.35  PJM’s proposed methodology 
to allocate costs to LSEs based on a single forecasting comparison, along with arbitrary 
discounts to data center loads, bears no meaningful relationship to reasonably-anticipated 
new data center load.  To the contrary, PJM’s proposal would allocate costs primarily based 
35
See, e.g., Building for the Future Through Electric Regional Transmission Planning and Cost 
Allocation, Order No. 1920-A, 189 FERC ¶ 61,126 at P 157 (Nov. 25, 2024) (Order No. 1920 mandates 
“consistent with long-established Commission and court precedent, that transmission customers within a 
transmission planning region need only pay costs that are ‘roughly commensurate’ with the benefits that 
transmission providers estimate they will receive from a regional transmission facility.”) (citations omitted).

13 
on LSEs with existing data center customers, rather than the new data center customers that 
are primarily driving the need for the RBP.  This disconnect between cost causers and 
beneficiaries and the RBP costs to be allocated will be magnified by PJM’s decision that 
the allocation will remain fixed for a fifteen-year period.  While cost allocation does not 
require absolute precision,  it does require an “articulable and plausible reason” to believe 
that the benefits received will be at least “roughly commensurate” with the costs.36  There 
is, however, no way to know what load conditions will look like in five years, much less 
fifteen.  Thus, there is no plausible reason to believe that PJM’s zonal cost allocation 
approach will ensure even a rough match between the costs and the beneficiaries of 
capacity procured in the RBP.37
PJM’s cost allocation proposal also violates the filed rate doctrine because it will 
undermine preexisting commercial relationships by attempting to allocate costs to data 
centers who possibly have already signed FERC-jurisdictional contracts based on a pre-
RBP understanding of the market.  As discussed above, PJM’s proposed allocation 
methodology could include data center facilities that already have binding commitments, 
including contracts between the data center customer and associated EDCs/LSEs.  Those 
contracts, to the extent they have been filed and accepted by the Commission, constitute 
the filed rate for those entities with respect to their energy supply obligations.  PJM’s 
proposal does not even recognize, much less attempt to justify, the need or reasonableness 
36
See Ill. Commerce Comm’n v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 477 (7th Cir. 2009).  See also Transmission 
Planning & Cost Allocation by Transmission Owning & Operating Pub. Utils., Order No. 1000, 136 FERC 
¶ 61,051 at P 622 (2011). 
37
This allocation mismatch is further compounded by PJM’s proposal to require non-defaulting LSEs 
to assume an additional payment obligation solely because another LSE failed to satisfy its allocated RBP 
Charges.  See Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD at Section 18.9(a).  The default of one LSE should not provide 
an independent basis for increasing the RBP costs assigned to another.

14 
of allocating these entities what would essentially constitute additional costs for the same 
service. 
PJM’s cost allocation proposal also fails to meet the requirements of FPA Section 
205 because the proposed LSE allocation methodologies are dependent in substantial part 
on whether and how certain state or other retail regulators choose to exercise their own 
authority and discretion.  There is no way to determine whether such allocations would be 
just and reasonable because such determination is left entirely to the discretion of state and 
other retail regulators.  The justness and reasonableness of a public utility’s proposal cannot 
be established based on speculative future action, particularly action by third-parties that 
neither PJM nor the Commission has the authority to control.38
Finally, PJM’s cost allocation proposal runs afoul of the “rule of reason” requiring 
that sufficient detail regarding FERC-jurisdictional services be included in a public utility’s 
tariff.  For example, in the affidavit accompanying PJM’s filing, PJM provides a chart with 
examples of possible RBP cost allocations.39  In this chart, FirstEnergy affiliate Potomac 
Edison is listed as an “Electric Distributor Zone/Area,” subject to cost allocation.  
However, the reference to Potomac Edison is unclear because there are multiple 
FirstEnergy affiliates operating under that banner across three different States.  This 
ambiguity suggests that FirstEnergy will have to decide how to sub-allocate the RBP costs 
among these entities, yet the PJM proposal does not even acknowledge, let alone provide 
details regarding the implementation of, this sub-allocation.  The Commission cannot 
38
See, e.g., N.Y. State Pub. Serv. Comm’n v. FERC, 104 F.4th 886 (D.C. Cir. 2024); N.Y. Indep. Sys. 
Operator, Inc., 183 FERC ¶ 61,130 (2023); Kan. Corp. Comm’n v. FERC, 881 F.3d 924 (D.C. Cir. 2018). 
39
See Attachment C, Affidavit of Ms. Danielle Croop at P 46 (“Croop Affidavit”).

15 
approve a rate filing that is so vague and subject to numerous implementation details that 
have yet to be even contemplated let alone developed. 
5.
PJM’s Reliability Backstop Procurement Should Be Limited to 
Resources That Most Effectively Address Reliability Needs. 
PJM proposes to permit a broad range of resources to participate in the RBP, 
including new generation resources, energy storage resources, demand response resources, 
and distributed energy resources.40  PJM justifies the RBP as an extraordinary measure 
necessary to address the approximately 6,831 MW capacity shortfall identified in the 
2028/2029 Base Residual Auction and to preserve resource adequacy within the PJM 
Region.41  Because the stated purpose of the procurement is to address an identified 
reliability need, the Commission should ensure that the procurement is structured to 
prioritize the resources that most effectively advance that need. 
While demand response, storage, and distributed energy resources may provide 
value under certain circumstances, not all eligible resource types provide the same level of 
reliability benefits or operational certainty.  Because the stated purpose of the RBP is to 
address a reliability shortfall, the Commission should ensure that the procurement 
appropriately prioritizes resources that provide firm and dependable capacity.  New 
dispatchable generation resources are capable of producing energy when needed and 
therefore provide a more direct means of addressing the resource adequacy concerns that 
PJM identifies as the basis for the proposal. 
Worth noting here is that the North American Electric Reliability Corporation 
(“NERC”)—which is responsible for developing, applying and enforcing mandatory 
40
July 31 RBP Proposal at 42 n.112. 
41
July 31 RBP Proposal at 31, 68.

16 
reliability standards—has identified that “conventional generators,” such as nuclear, coal 
and natural gas generators, provide much of the essential reliability services that support 
reliable operation of the grid today.42  NERC further reports that wind and solar resources 
lack the spinning mass, that is, the traditional excitation systems, that provide for voltage 
control and stability to support the transmission grid.43  NERC explains that generators that 
can be controlled, that is, dispatched on demand, provide system inertia, dynamic reactive 
support, and frequency response for stable grid operation.44  In an era that is dominated by 
affordability concerns, it would be reasonable to conclude that scarce customer dollars 
should be directed to resources that provide or reflect the dispatchable characteristics that 
are necessary for reliability. 
This issue is particularly important given the magnitude of the procurement and the 
fifteen-year commitments associated with selected resources.45  PJM expressly states that

constraint.46  Although cost discipline is important, a procurement justified on reliability 
grounds should not focus exclusively on minimizing costs without sufficient consideration 
of the relative reliability value provided by different resource types.

tailored to procure the resources that most effectively address reliability needs.  At a

6.
PJM’s Proposed Implementation Schedule Is Unreasonably 
Compressed. 
PJM proposes to commence the Reliability Backstop Procurement on September 
30, 2026 and requests that the Commission act on the filing by September 29, 2026.47
PJM’s proposed schedule would therefore permit the procurement to begin immediately 
following Commission approval.  While FirstEnergy appreciates the need for prompt 
action, PJM’s proposed implementation schedule provides insufficient time for affected 
LSEs, Electric Distributors, state regulators, and retail customers to evaluate the 
consequences of the proposal and take steps to mitigate resulting obligations.  The RBP is 
not a minor modification to PJM’s capacity construct, but an entirely new procurement 
mechanism.  The RBP will create substantial long-term payment obligations, impose 
unprecedented collateral requirements, and rely upon state-specific cost-allocation 
determinations that, in many jurisdictions, have not yet been developed.48  For these 
reasons, PJM has failed to demonstrate that the compressed timeline is just and reasonable. 
PJM acknowledges that implementation of its proposal requires substantial 
coordination among PJM, Electric Distributors, states, Regional Electric Reliability

The compressed schedule is particularly problematic given the magnitude of the 
financial obligations at issue.  As discussed above, PJM proposes to require LSEs allocated 
RBP costs to post hundreds of millions of dollars collateral.  FirstEnergy’s affiliates alone 
estimate the collateral costs for their retail customers could be in excess of $350 million.  
Before such obligations are imposed, affected entities should have a reasonable opportunity

allocation framework and associated collateral requirements. 
Here, PJM has failed to demonstrate that its compressed implementation schedule 
is just and reasonable.  Although PJM cites the 2028/2029 Delivery Year resource 
adequacy shortfall as the basis for the proposal, PJM has not shown that delaying 
commencement of the procurement for a reasonable period would undermine the stated 
objectives of the RBP.  Indeed, PJM’s tariff contemplates a RBP-like procurement only 
occurring after three years of resource adequacy shortfalls, while only two have occurred

7.
PJM’s Proposed “Opt-Out” Mechanism Will Allow 
Unreasonable Cost Shifting Among Load Customers. 
With regard to Electric Distributors, PJM proposes to reduce the Initial RBP Target 
based on requests from certain Electric Distributors, such as municipal utilities and 
cooperatives, to “opt out.”51  Thus, an Electric Distributor whose territory qualifies for an 
“opt out” relating to capacity procurement will not have any cost responsibility assigned to 
it.  Such an “opt out” is unduly discriminatory under FPA Section 205 and therefore cannot 
be approved.  Large load in those territories eligible for the “opt out” is no less real than 
large load in any other territory, and PJM provides no reasonable basis for treating such 
loads differently under the RBP.  The proposed ”opt out” is also inconsistent with cost-
causation principles because it will result in customers in other territories subsidizing

8. 
PJM Should Strengthen Supplier Performance and Credit 
Requirements. 
The Commission should ensure that customers are adequately protected against 
supplier non-performance over the fifteen-year commitment term.  While PJM proposes 
numerous measures intended to reduce development risk and increase the likelihood that 
selected resources achieve commercial operation, those protections are directed primarily 
toward construction risk and the risk that a resource fails to come online in the first 
instance.52  For example, PJM proposes to assess an RBP UCAP MW shortfall charge when 
a committed resource fails to achieve commercial operation and provide committed 
capacity.53  PJM further proposes that a resource’s commitment may ultimately be 
rescinded if the resource fails to provide any committed RBP UCAP MW after three 
consecutive Delivery Years.54  These provisions help address development risk, but they 
again do not fully protect customers against the possibility that a resource satisfies its initial 
commercial operation obligations and subsequently underperforms during the balance of 
its fifteen-year commitment term. 
This concern is particularly significant because the RBP would provide selected 
suppliers with long-term, customer-supported revenue streams extending for up to fifteen 
years.55  LSEs, and ultimately retail customers, will remain responsible for funding those

Response Resources. 
PJM must clarify how its proposed gating criteria apply to demand response 
resources.  As drafted, the proposal appears to require only a contract or agreement 
evidencing a “plan or evidence of deployed enabling infrastructure,” not a contract or 
agreement demonstrating a clear and binding commitment to provide the MWs sold into 
the RBP.56
That ambiguity is significant.  If demand response resources may satisfy the gating 
criteria based merely on a “plan,” rather than a binding commitment for the underlying
